value_chain_position: Transformers-and-switchgear layer of the electrification and grid chain -- a named anchor example. Powell builds medium- and high-voltage switchgear, motor control centres and complete pre-fabricated power-control rooms, and sells them to electric utilities, oil-and-gas and petrochemical operators, and, increasingly, data-centre developers.
cost_curve_verified: There is no unit-cost curve for an equipment maker, so the load-bearing proxies are cash conversion and leverage, and both AGREE with the company-reported figures. The input bundle's free-cash-flow margin of 21.08% matches the filed statements exactly: trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of $243.96 million on $1,157.5 million of revenue is 21.1% (quarterly filings through 30 June 2026, filed 4 August 2026). The bundle's revenue growth of 7.0% is consistent with the company's reported +9% year over year in the June-2026 quarter and +6.6% across the first nine months of fiscal 2026. One mild DISAGREEMENT: the bundle carries net debt to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of -2.27 times, while the filed balance sheet gives -2.53 times ($631.0 million of net cash against $249.0 million of trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) -- the direction is identical and the difference is immaterial. The figure that does need correcting is not in the proxies at all: about $263 million of the cash balance arrived in the June quarter as customer advances on the $400 million-plus data-centre order, so the net cash is not all surplus.
gm_trajectory: Expanding for three years, flat for the last two quarters. Annual gross margin went 15.96% in fiscal 2022, 21.10% in 2023, 26.98% in 2024 and 29.37% in 2025 -- an expansion of 1,341 basis points. But in the June-2026 quarter gross margin was 30.57% against 30.71% a year earlier, down 14 basis points on 9% revenue growth, the second consecutive quarter of slight year-over-year compression (the March quarter was 29.65% against 29.94%). Management now guides margins merely to 'maintain levels consistent to the trailing twelve months' -- about 30.1% -- and has said roughly 150 to 170 basis points of the reported figure comes from project closeout true-ups rather than as-sold work. Growing revenue at a flat margin is a good business, not a pricing-power business.
bull_thesis:
Powell Industries is the purest small-capitalisation way to own the physical bottleneck of the artificial-intelligence power build-out, and the order book has just proved it in the most emphatic way available. In the quarter ended 30 June 2026, reported on 3 August, the company booked $934 million of new orders, up 158% year over year, against $311.7 million of revenue -- a book-to-bill ratio (orders won divided by revenue billed) of 3.0 times. Backlog reached $2.4 billion, up 69% year over year and 35% sequentially, the first time above $2 billion in the company's 79-year history, and equal to 2.07 years of current revenue. That is contracted work, not a pipeline: Powell books into backlog only on firm award, and the quarter contained three individually disclosed mega orders -- a behind-the-meter data-centre campus in excess of $400 million, a roughly $75 million petrochemical and fertiliser award, and a roughly $60 million liquefied-natural-gas award.

The second leg is that this is no longer the oil-and-gas fabricator the market used to own. In the June quarter, commercial and other industrial revenue (which is mostly data centres) grew 54% and electric utility grew 18%, while petrochemical fell 49% -- and the company still grew 9% in aggregate. Five years ago utility and commercial together were under 20% of backlog; by March 2026 electric utility was 30% of backlog, oil and gas excluding petrochemical 29%, and commercial and other industrial 29%. Management earned that shift over a decade of deliberate investment, and the chief executive's description of the change in customer relationships -- conversations 'much more strategic today than I think fair to say ever in Powell's history' (May 2025) -- is corroborated by the largest utility award in company history, a greater-than-one-gigawatt generation facility booked in the September-2025 quarter.

The third leg is the economics of the transition. Gross margin has expanded 1,341 basis points in three years, to about 30%. Return on invested capital has gone from effectively zero in fiscal 2021 to 13.8%, comfortably ahead of Eaton at 9.1%, Hubbell at 9.6% and nVent at 10.7%, on a balance sheet carrying almost no goodwill. Trailing free cash flow is $244.0 million on capital expenditure of only $12.2 million -- barely 1% of revenue -- so growth here is not bought with capital. Net cash is $631.0 million against $2.5 million of total debt, which means the company can fund the $70 million to $100 million greenfield plant it is evaluating, the $8 million fabrication investment, the leased bridge facilities and continued small acquisitions entirely from its own resources.

The fourth leg is capacity, which is the current constraint and therefore the current opportunity. The chief executive said plainly in May 2026 that Powell cannot meet every schedule coming in the door. The Jacintoport expansion (335,000 square feet, $12.4 million) completes by the close of fiscal 2026. A leased bridge facility reaches productive capacity in about six months and a greenfield plant in about two years, and management sizes the incremental revenue capacity at $100 million to $250 million. If the board commits -- a decision it has said is 'just about there' -- the revenue conversion rate on a $2.4 billion book steps up materially in fiscal 2027 and 2028.

Finally, management is credible. In August 2025 the chief financial officer volunteered that reported margins contained about 150 basis points of closeout gains and that the as-sold margin in backlog was lower; the chief executive said project pricing was 'a little softer' prospectively. Both statements proved accurate a year later. A management team that talks its own numbers down when results are good is unusual and valuable.

Conditions this case depends on: the board commits the greenfield or bridging capacity within two quarters and it comes in on schedule, as the last two expansions did; the $400 million-plus data-centre customer proceeds to later phases; the copper hedging programme holds gross margin near 30% through a two-year fixed-price backlog; and revenue growth accelerates from single digits toward the 20%-plus rate the order book implies. On roughly $1.5 billion of fiscal-2027 revenue at a 22% margin on earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, that is about $7.00 of earnings per share, and the shares are worth about $262.
bear_thesis:
The demand argument is won and fully paid for; the conversion argument is unresolved and the price allows nothing for failing it. At $211.06 the shares carry about 40 times trailing earnings of $5.22, about 28.5 times trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of $249.0 million, and about 6.1 times trailing revenue on an enterprise value of roughly $7.09 billion. Those are not discount multiples: Hubbell trades at 21.4 times and 5.04 times, nVent at 27.5 times and 5.74 times, Eaton at 31.8 times and 6.41 times. Powell is at the middle of that band while being the smallest, lumpiest and most project-dependent business in it -- and the one whose earnings actually went to zero in the last downturn ($631 thousand of net income on $471 million of revenue in fiscal 2021).

The pricing-power leg is already breaking. Gross margin in the June-2026 quarter was 30.57% against 30.71% a year earlier, the second straight quarter of slight year-over-year compression, and this on a quarter when orders tripled. A supplier with genuine scarcity power raises price into a demand shock. Powell did not, and its own chief executive explained why in August 2025: 'the pricing is not improving... it would be difficult for me to say we could take more there.' Management now guides margin flat at the trailing-twelve-month level of about 30.1%, of which roughly 150 to 170 basis points is project closeout true-ups. Strip those and the as-sold margin in that $2.4 billion backlog is nearer 28.5%. The market is capitalising a 30% margin that management has told it not to expect to improve.

Commodities are an input cost here, and the exposure has just lengthened. Copper, steel and aluminium are the raw material of switchgear, and the backlog now stretches into fiscal 2028 at largely fixed prices. The hedging programme is, in the chief financial officer's own words, 'an insurance policy to protect the margins that we have in backlog' -- insurance is bought term by term, and a two-year fixed-price book has a long un-hedged tail. A sustained copper spike of the kind an analyst already flagged in May 2026 would take 150 to 300 basis points off gross margin on work that cannot be repriced. Add lead-acid batteries and other bought-out content that management concedes 'will come over overseas' and is 'subject to some risk' from tariffs.

The order book itself carries concentration and cancellation risk that is not being priced. One unnamed counterparty accounts for roughly a sixth of the $2.4 billion backlog through a behind-the-meter data-centre campus whose later phases are not contracted. Powell's customer is not disclosed, the termination terms are not disclosed, and no analyst has asked. If the artificial-intelligence build-out enters a digestion phase -- and the hyperscaler capital-spending cycle has never yet been tested by one -- a single decision descopes or delays more revenue than Powell earned in all of fiscal 2025. Petrochemical revenue, meanwhile, is already down 49% year over year, which is what an end market rolling over actually looks like while management calls it 'the early stages of a cyclical inflection.'

Then there is execution. Book-to-bill of 3.0 times against capital expenditure of 1.05% of revenue is a company filling an order book faster than it can build the factories to empty it. Revenue grew 4%, 6% and 9% in the last three quarters while orders grew 63%, 65% and 158%. The greenfield decision has been 'a couple of weeks' from the board twice. A greenfield plant is 'conservatively, two years' away, and even the leased bridge is six months to productive capacity, before which Powell is hiring engineers into a market where the chief executive concedes 'we do have some needs that are challenging us.' Engineered-to-order project houses that scale headcount and outsourcing fast are exactly where cost overruns and closeout reversals appear -- and closeouts are currently a positive 170 basis points that can turn negative.

The balance sheet is weaker than it prints. Customer advances rose about $263 million in the June quarter alone, and the chief financial officer said in February 2026 that 40% to 50% of the cash balance is working capital committed to the backlog, leaving only $200 million to $225 million genuinely free against a then-$1.6 billion book. Scaled up, the true surplus today is perhaps $250 million to $300 million, not $631 million. Anyone adding the full net cash to an operating value is counting the customers' money twice.

Finally, nobody inside the company has bought a share. Across the entire move from a 52-week low of $69 to a high of $328, the filings show zero open-market purchases against 67 disposals totalling 157,234 shares -- 90,093 shares disposed in the first calendar quarter of 2026 against 7,100 acquired, and 61,463 disposed against nothing acquired in the second. What would confirm the bear case: a quarter with gross margin below 29%, or book-to-bill falling back under 1.0 times, or a negative closeout true-up, or the greenfield decision deferred again. On roughly $1.2 billion of fiscal-2027 revenue at a 17% margin on earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, this is a $96 stock.

risk_reward: Poor at today's level, because the base case sits below the price. The shares trade at $211.06; the reconciled base-case sum-of-the-parts is about $188, so there is no upside to fair value at all -- the market is paying a premium of roughly $23 a share above what the parts support. The favourable case is $262 and the adverse case is $96. In other words the investor is being offered a modest gain if a capacity build he has not yet been shown goes right, against a very large loss if the data-centre order cycle digests, copper bites the fixed-price backlog, or closeout true-ups reverse. There is no structural floor: net cash is only about $17.25 per share and book value about $20.68, neither of which is anywhere near the price, and there is no deal, tender or contractual downside protection. The asymmetry becomes attractive nearer $150 to $160, roughly a 20% discount to the base case.
catalyst_status_note: The load-bearing event has already happened. The single largest award in the company's 79-year history -- a behind-the-meter data-centre campus in excess of $400 million -- was first disclosed on the 5 May 2026 earnings call as a post-quarter event, and was formally booked into orders and backlog in the quarter reported on 3 August 2026 (new orders $934 million, up 158%; backlog $2.4 billion, up 69%; book-to-bill 3.0 times, per the company's results release of 3 August 2026 and the quarterly filing accepted 4 August 2026). The fiscal third-quarter print itself, the other candidate event, was released after the close on 3 August 2026 and the call was held on 4 August 2026. Both are spent. Under this lane's rules a spent event is neither a plus nor a penalty -- the verdict below rests entirely on the residual value case, and the residual value case is what fails. The remaining unfired item worth tracking is not a catalyst in this sense: the board's decision on a $70 million to $100 million greenfield plant, which management has described as imminent for two consecutive quarters without dating it.
peer_comps_note: Measured against the assigned chain competitors on 4 August 2026, Powell is priced at the middle of the pack while being the smallest and least diversified member of it. On enterprise value to trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: Powell 28.5 times, against Hubbell 21.4, nVent 27.5, Eaton 31.8 and Argan 44.3 -- a peer median of about 29.6 times. On enterprise value to trailing revenue: Powell 6.1 times against Hubbell 5.0, nVent 5.7, Eaton 6.4 and Argan 8.0. Powell's defence is returns: 13.8% return on invested capital against Eaton's 9.1%, Hubbell's 9.6% and nVent's 10.7%, achieved on a balance sheet with $6.0 million of goodwill rather than the 58% to 64% intangible-heavy asset bases the larger three carry. The offsetting case is business quality: Eaton, Hubbell and nVent sell repeatable products with aftermarket revenue, while roughly two thirds of Powell's revenue is engineered-to-order project work whose trough earnings were demonstrably near zero as recently as fiscal 2021. Argan's 44 times is not a usable comparison for a manufacturer -- it is an asset-light engineering and construction contractor with a 27.6% return on invested capital and almost no inventory. The honest conclusion is that Powell deserves roughly a peer multiple, not a premium, and it already has one. The European names in the chain map (ABB, Schneider Electric, Siemens Energy) were not priced here; all three are far larger and are competitors rather than valuation anchors for a $7.7 billion company.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about demand -- it is about the two steps between an order and a dollar of profit.

First, the street is capitalising a gross margin that management has explicitly told it not to expect to improve. Sell-side notes and the stock's rating through the first half of 2026 treated the 1,341 basis points of gross-margin expansion since fiscal 2022 as a trend. It stopped. The June-2026 quarter printed 30.57% against 30.71% a year earlier, and the March quarter 29.65% against 29.94% -- two consecutive quarters of slight year-over-year compression, achieved in a period when orders tripled. The company's own guidance on 3 August 2026 is that 'gross margins will maintain levels consistent to the trailing twelve months,' about 30.1%. More pointedly, in August 2025 the chief financial officer disclosed that reported margins carried roughly 150 basis points of project closeout gains and that stripping those 'should approximate the as-sold margins that we see in our $1.4 billion backlog' -- so the underlying margin on the work now in hand is closer to 28.5%. The market is valuing 30% and management has documented 28.5%.

Second, the street is treating the order book as though it converts on a normal schedule. It does not, because Powell cannot build it fast enough. Over the last three quarters orders grew 63%, 65% and 158% while revenue grew 4%, 6% and 9%. Trailing capital expenditure is $12.2 million, or 1.05% of revenue, against a 3.0-times book-to-bill. The chief executive said in May 2026, when asked directly whether the company was turning work away: 'Are we able to meet the schedules of everything coming in the door? The answer is no.' The greenfield plant that would fix this is 'conservatively, two years' away and has not been approved; a leased bridge is six months from productive capacity and has not been signed. A $2.4 billion backlog with no factory to run it through is a slower asset than the multiple implies.

Third, the street is adding the wrong cash number. Powell's $631.0 million of net cash is being treated as a clean deduction from enterprise value. About $263 million of it arrived in the June quarter alone as customer advances and billings in excess of costs, precisely as the $400 million-plus data-centre order landed. The chief financial officer told investors in February 2026 that 40% to 50% of the balance would be 'deployed at some point in the future to that $1.6 billion backlog,' leaving 'probably $200 million to $225 million' genuinely free. That is roughly $300 million today, not $631 million -- a difference of about $9 per share.

Fourth, and least appreciated, is the input-cost exposure. Copper, steel and aluminium are the raw material of switchgear, and Powell's visibility now stretches into fiscal 2028 on largely fixed prices. The hedging programme is described by the chief financial officer as 'an insurance policy to protect the margins that we have in backlog' -- which is accurate and which is exactly why the far end of a two-year book is exposed. An analyst raised 'the spike in metal prices in 2026' on the May 2026 call and did not follow up. Rising copper is a margin headwind for this business, never a revenue tailwind, and the longer the backlog gets the more of it is un-repriceable.

Where the street is right, and we agree: the demand is real, the diversification out of hydrocarbons is verified in the segment growth rates, the balance sheet is genuinely unlevered, and management is credible. Our disagreement is entirely with the price. The remaining published targets -- a single $333 from Roth's Chip Moore dated 6 May 2026, set when the stock was $317 -- represent one analyst, not a street view, and that target is now 90 days stale and predates both the June-quarter miss and the 36% decline from the $328 high.
valley_of_death:
The risky window here is the next three to nine months, and it is a conversion-and-cost window rather than a solvency one. Powell has $631.0 million of net cash against $2.5 million of total debt and generated $244.0 million of free cash in the last twelve months. There is no maturity wall, no burn, no financing need, and the dividend of $0.09 a quarter costs about $13 million a year against $244 million of free cash. Nothing here threatens the company. What threatens the shares is this:

One -- the September-2026 quarter, reported in mid-November, is the first that must show revenue accelerating. The June quarter already missed on both lines ($311.7 million against $316.9 million expected, $1.42 against $1.49). Jacintoport's 335,000 square feet completes 'by the close of Fiscal 2026,' meaning the capacity arrives at the end of the quarter, not during it. Consensus is modelling roughly 26% forward earnings growth. A second consecutive single-digit revenue quarter against a 3.0-times book-to-bill would force the market to re-price the conversion assumption directly, and there is no cushion in a 40-times trailing multiple.

Two -- the closeout reversal risk. Project closeout true-ups added 1.7% of revenue to fiscal-2025 margins and management expects 'some project closeouts in a favourable fashion in 2026.' These are estimates trued up at completion, and they run both ways. Powell is simultaneously hiring engineers into a market where the chief executive concedes shortages, standing up two satellite engineering centres, outsourcing substation fabrication, and executing the largest project in its history across multiple divisions and countries. That is precisely the configuration in which a project house books a negative true-up. One bad quarter of closeouts is 150 to 200 basis points of gross margin.

Three -- input costs. The un-hedged tail of a backlog now extending into fiscal 2028 meets a copper market an analyst already described as spiking in 2026. A 150 to 300 basis-point margin hit on fixed-price work is entirely plausible within this window and cannot be passed through.

Four -- the capacity decision cuts both ways. If the board approves the $70 million to $100 million greenfield plant, free cash flow drops sharply for two years and the market must digest a capital-intensity story from a company it has valued as capital-light. If the board defers again -- the third deferral -- the conversion thesis loses its last support. There is no comfortable version of this announcement at today's price.

Five -- petrochemical revenue is down 49% year over year and management's claimed 'early stages of a cyclical inflection' has not appeared in the numbers for three quarters. That is a live drag on the September and December quarters regardless of what data centres do.
positioning_washout:
The forced-selling pressure here is momentum-driven, not income-driven, and it is already underway.

There is no yield-focused shareholder base to dislodge: the dividend is $0.09 a quarter, a yield of about 0.17%, and it has not been cut -- the board declared it again on 3 August 2026, payable 16 September. Nobody owns this stock for income. Leverage-driven forced selling is impossible: there is essentially no debt and no covenant.

What does exist is a crowded momentum and thematic position that is unwinding mechanically. The shares went from a 52-week low of $69 to a high of $328 and are now $211.06 -- down roughly 36% from the high, 20% below the 50-day average of $263.97, and only 11% above the 200-day of $190.63. A three-for-one split completed in the June quarter, heavy retail and search interest is evident in the steady stream of 'most searched stock' coverage through July, and there has been a series of one-day moves of 9.6% down (26 June), 4.5% down (16 July) and 8.3% down (28 July) before the print. On 4 August the shares opened at $191.25 against a prior close of $219.72 -- a 13% gap -- and recovered to $211.06 intraday. That pattern, a violent gap and a same-day recovery on an earnings miss with record orders, is the signature of a shareholder base split between thematic momentum money exiting and value-seeking money arriving. It is not a capitulation low; capitulation does not bounce 10% off the open.

The 200-day average at $190.63 is the level that matters mechanically. A close below it would remove the last technical support for the trend-following cohort and is the most likely trigger for the genuine flush -- which, on our numbers, would take the shares toward the $150 to $160 area where the risk and reward become attractive.

One further signal on positioning, from the inside: across the entire run from $69 to $328 the filings show zero open-market purchases by officers or directors against 67 disposals totalling 157,234 shares, including 90,093 shares disposed in the first calendar quarter of 2026 and 61,463 in the second with nothing acquired. Much of that is routine vesting-related selling and should not be over-read, but the absence of a single open-market purchase during a 36% decline is a notable non-event.
forcing_function:
There is no dated, binding event that forces a re-rating in Powell's favour, and that is an honest description of the setup rather than a criticism of it -- this lane does not require one. The events that will actually move the shares are these, in order of importance.

First, the fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 results, due in mid-November 2026 based on the company's consistent pattern (19 November 2025, 20 November 2024). This is the print that must show revenue accelerating out of the single digits, because Jacintoport's 335,000 square feet completes 'by the close of Fiscal 2026' and there is no longer a capacity excuse afterwards. It is also the print that carries the annual report, in which the exact backlog conversion percentage is disclosed -- the number to watch is what share of $2.4 billion is convertible in the next twelve months, against the 60% Powell has disclosed for the last two years. A materially lower figure means the backlog is lengthening rather than accelerating.

Second, the board's capacity decision. Management said in May 2026 that a choice between a $70 million to $100 million greenfield plant and a leased bridge would come 'within the next few quarters,' and that it was 'just about there.' This is an undated corporate decision, not a scheduled event, and it has already slipped past two board meetings. Approval would be the clearest signal that the $2.4 billion book converts; a third deferral would be the clearest signal that it does not.

Third, disclosure of the data-centre counterparty. Roughly a sixth of the backlog sits with one unnamed customer on a multi-phase campus. A phase-two award, or the customer's own capital-spending announcement, would either de-risk or expose that concentration. No date attaches to this.

Fourth, and mechanically the nearest, the 200-day moving average at $190.63. It is not a corporate event, but it is the level at which the remaining momentum holders are likely to be forced out, and it is the practical gateway to the entry level named below.
moderator_conclusion:
Powell Industries is a genuinely good company at a price that has already paid for several years of successful execution, and our conclusion is to wait rather than to buy.

Start with what is not in doubt. The June-2026 quarter produced $934 million of new orders against $311.7 million of revenue -- three dollars of work won for every dollar billed -- and lifted the order book to $2.4 billion, up 69% year over year and equal to more than two years of current revenue. The composition of that book has genuinely changed: electric utility and commercial work, under 20% of backlog five years ago, are now the majority, and in the June quarter commercial and other industrial revenue grew 54% and electric utility 18% while petrochemical fell 49%. The balance sheet carries $631.0 million of net cash against $2.5 million of debt, return on invested capital has climbed from effectively zero in fiscal 2021 to 13.8% -- better than Eaton, Hubbell or nVent -- and management has a documented habit of telling investors the unflattering thing before the numbers do. This is a clean franchise with a strengthening trajectory, and nothing in the forensic file suggests otherwise.

The problem is arithmetic. At $211.06 the shares carry about 40 times trailing earnings, 28.5 times trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and 6.1 times revenue -- the middle of a peer band running from Hubbell at 21.4 times to Argan at 44.3 times, for the smallest and lumpiest business in the group and the only one whose earnings actually went to zero in the last downturn. Valuing the segments separately against those same peers, and crediting only the genuinely surplus portion of the cash rather than the customers' advances, gives a base-case fair value of about $188 per share. That is below the market price. There is no discount here to buy.

Two operating facts explain why we will not stretch. The gross margin, which is the lie detector for pricing power in a supply-constrained niche, has stopped expanding: 30.57% in the June quarter against 30.71% a year earlier, the second consecutive quarter of slight year-over-year compression, in a period when orders tripled. A company with real scarcity power raises price into a demand shock; Powell's own chief executive said it could not. Management now guides margin flat, and roughly 150 basis points of the reported figure is project closeout true-ups rather than as-sold work. And the order book is filling faster than the factories can empty it -- capital expenditure of 1.05% of revenue against a 3.0-times book-to-bill, revenue growing 4%, 6% and 9% while orders grew 63%, 65% and 158%, and a greenfield plant that is two years out and still unapproved after two board meetings. Every dollar of that $2.4 billion has to pass through a building that does not exist yet.

The commodity exposure runs the wrong way for a bull, as it always does for an equipment maker: copper, steel and aluminium are input costs, the backlog now stretches into fiscal 2028 at largely fixed prices, and the hedging programme by its own description protects the margins already in the book rather than the far tail of it.

So this is a wait-for-the-wash-out, not a pass and not a buy. The business qualifies; the price does not, and the price is above our fair value rather than merely close to it. Two specific things would change the answer. On price: a close below the 200-day average of $190.63 followed by a flush into the $150 to $160 area, which is roughly a 20% discount to our $188 base case and the level at which the adverse case stops dominating the arithmetic. On fundamentals: a quarter that pairs gross margin back above 31% with revenue growth accelerating into the mid-teens, which would prove that the capacity is converting and the pricing leg is intact -- at which point a higher price would be justified on better facts. Absent one of those, the risk and reward on offer is a modest gain for a build that has not been approved against a very large loss if the data-centre order cycle takes a breath.

One last note on the event calendar, which does not drive this verdict: the load-bearing catalyst -- the largest award in the company's history, a data-centre campus in excess of $400 million -- has already been announced and already been booked. Under this lane's rules a spent event is neither a plus nor a penalty, and it changes nothing here. The verdict rests on the residual value case, and the residual value case is simply that the shares cost more than the parts are worth.
